name: Paul's undisputed letters
summary: Seven letters are widely accepted as Paul's own. They predate the written Gospels and preserve earlier formulas about Jesus' death, burial, resurrection appearances, followers, and brother James.
establishes: Jesus was remembered as a recent Jewish man who was crucified
Peter, James, the Twelve, and other followers were known by name
resurrection appearances were being proclaimed before Paul's letters
limits: Paul writes as a committed apostle, not a detached biographer. His letters establish early belief and named relationships; they do not independently verify a miracle.

name: The Gospel of Mark
summary: Mark is generally dated around AD 70 and is the earliest complete Gospel that survives. It gathers earlier oral and written traditions into a continuous account of Jesus' ministry and death.
establishes: a developed Jesus tradition existed by the first Jewish–Roman war
Jesus was placed firmly in Galilee, Judea, and the rule of Pilate
the crucifixion stood at the center of the earliest surviving narrative
limits: Mark is anonymous in the text and written to form faith as well as preserve memory. Individual episodes still require source criticism rather than automatic acceptance.

name: Matthew and Luke
assessment: Later Synoptic witnesses using earlier material
summary: Matthew and Luke both use Mark while adding other sayings, stories, genealogies, and community memories. Their agreements can reflect shared dependence; their differences reveal distinct sources and theological aims.
establishes: multiple streams of Jesus tradition circulated beyond Mark
communities preserved overlapping sayings and episodes
the movement interpreted Jesus within different Jewish and Gentile settings
limits: Three Gospels are not three independent witnesses at every point. Dependence on Mark must be separated from genuinely distinct material.

name: The Gospel of John
summary: John presents a markedly different chronology, voice, and theological portrait while retaining the same broad setting: a Jewish Jesus, followers, conflict in Judea, and death under Pilate.
establishes: a distinct stream of Jesus memory circulated by the late first century
core people and the execution setting overlap with the Synoptic tradition
claims about Jesus' identity developed in explicit theological language
limits: John's long speeches and chronology cannot simply be harmonized with the Synoptics. Historical use requires attention to the Gospel's later theological form.
